claims.paraphrase: The specification assigns model-theoretic truth conditions to RDF graphs and RDF/RDFS vocabularies, characterizing truth-preserving transformations and derivations.
Passages are normative except sections explicitly marked non-normative and authoring guidelines, diagrams, examples and notes.
Capitalized requirement keywords have their RFC 2119 meanings.
Normative authority concerns RDF semantics and inference validity; social naming conventions and relationships to non-RDF Web content are outside the specified semantics.
Additional semantic assumptions about an RDF vocabulary constitute a semantic extension and determine an entailment regime.
Extensions may restrict legal graph syntax and treat violations as errors; none of the extensions normatively defined here adds such graph restrictions.
Whenever G simply entails H, every extension must preserve that entailment if its additional syntactic conditions hold; stronger semantics cannot cancel an accepted simple entailment.
IRI, triple, graph, subject, predicate, object, RDF source, node, blank node, literal, graph isomorphism and dataset have their Concepts meanings.
An RDF graph is a set of RDF triples, using RDF-term identity for its triple components.
claims.formalization_note: A list implementation may represent a graph through its membership set; this definition alone does not establish a unique enumeration or a correct cardinality operation.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: An RDF graph G is a set of RDF triples; equality of G is equality of membership.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Concepts supplies the term domains; their concrete lexical constraints remain open.

claims.paraphrase: An ordinary RDF triple has an IRI or blank-node subject, an IRI predicate, and an IRI, blank-node or literal object; those term kinds are distinct.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: An ordinary RDF triple has subject in IRI or Blank, predicate in IRI, and object in IRI or Literal or Blank.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Disjoint syntactic categories are enforced. IRI and Literal are abstract domains, not validated concrete strings.

claims.paraphrase: Abstract IRI and literal identity follow Concepts, not equality of denoted values; blank-node identifiers are concrete-syntax labels rather than the abstract blank nodes themselves.
claims.formalization_note: Check literal language-tag identity against Concepts separately from the lowercase language-tag value condition in section 7.1.

claims.paraphrase: All definitions apply unchanged to generalized triples, graphs and datasets, whose triple positions can each contain any RDF term.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A generalized triple permits any RDF term in each of its three positions; a generalized graph is a set of generalized triples.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Ordinary graphs embed into generalized graphs. Instance and interpolation claims for generalized syntax have not been discharged.

claims.paraphrase: An interpretation maps IRIs and literals into a semantic domain subject to constraints; qualified kinds of interpretation determine corresponding entailment regimes.

Denoting and referring name the interpretation-dependent relationship to a referent; identifying denotes an externally established naming relationship, which need not agree with a particular interpretation.
Equality denotes strict identity, and angle-bracket pairs are ordered pairs; these conventions apply throughout the mathematics.
A name is an IRI or literal; a typed literal contributes itself and its datatype IRI as names, and a vocabulary is a set of names.
The empty graph is the empty set of triples.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The empty graph contains no triples.

claims.paraphrase: Subgraphs and proper subgraphs are respectively subsets and proper subsets of triples; a triple is identified with its singleton subgraph.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: H is a subgraph of G exactly when every member of H is a member of G.

claims.paraphrase: A ground graph has no blank nodes.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: G is ground exactly when no blank node occurs in any triple of G.

claims.paraphrase: An instance is obtained by consistently replacing some or all blank nodes through a function into RDF terms; names already in the graph are unchanged.
Instantiation is reflexive and composes transitively; every resulting triple is an instance of at least one original triple.
An instance relative to vocabulary V uses only names in V for substituted names; substitutions by blank nodes are still permitted.
An instance is proper if some blank node becomes a name or distinct blank nodes are identified by the substitution.
Graph isomorphism is an invertible renaming of blank nodes, leaving names fixed; isomorphic graphs are mutual instances and may be treated as identical up to that renaming.
A graph is lean if none of its instances is a proper subgraph of itself.
A non-lean graph is logically redundant relative to its lean subgraphs; every ground graph is lean.
Repeated occurrences of the identical triple do not add graph members, and order does not distinguish graphs with the same members.
claims.formalization_note: This is the mathematical consequence of sethood, not a separately coded entailment rule or a requirement to reject duplicate surface-syntax statements.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every set G, G union G equals G; repeated occurrences of a triple in an input list denote the same set as one occurrence.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: This is a mathematical consequence of the set definition, not a separately labelled W3C rule.

claims.paraphrase: Blank-node sharing between graphs requires a source structure that provides for shared identity; repeated retrieval of the same document or source does not by itself identify its blank nodes.
Applications manipulating scoped blank-node labels should track the abstract identities and rename labels when combining sources to prevent accidental conflation.
claims.formalization_note: This is an authoring/implementation guideline under the section 2 exception, not a new truth condition.

claims.paraphrase: Graph union uses triple-set union and preserves actual blank-node identities, including identities shared across inputs.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The union of G and H contains a triple exactly when G or H contains that triple, preserving blank-node identity.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Binary union; arbitrary families are not yet implemented.

claims.paraphrase: Merge first separates blank nodes shared between inputs, then takes their union; merging subgraphs can therefore produce a larger graph.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: The binary merge of G and H takes their union after placing their blank nodes in disjoint copies. I satisfies that merge exactly when I satisfies G and I satisfies H.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Uses Sum B₁ B₂ for fresh identities. This is a representative up to blank-node renaming; literal equality to union for already-disjoint domains is not asserted.

claims.paraphrase: The union is an instance of the merge; when inputs share no blank nodes, union and merge coincide. Union retains the joint content, including shared blank-node meaning.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For any G and H with a common blank-node domain, their union simply entails their merge.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Semantic consequence only. The stated syntactic instance relation and no-shared-nodes equality remain open.

claims.paraphrase: All semantic extensions must preserve the simple truth conditions; they may add constraints but must not modify or negate those conditions.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For an extension represented by additional conditions C on simple interpretations, simple entailment implies entailment under C.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Models only extensions over this graph syntax; does not formalize every permitted higher-level notation.

claims.paraphrase: Semantics applies to a graph rather than a changing RDF source; a source is interpreted through its graph value at a time or state, while a fixed graph does not change meaning with time.
A simple interpretation includes a nonempty resource set IR.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 1

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IR is a nonempty set of resources.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: IR and IP are predicates on an ambient type U; no finiteness assumption.

claims.paraphrase: A simple interpretation includes a property set IP.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 2

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IP is a set of properties, permitted to overlap IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: No IP subset IR constraint is imposed in simple interpretations.

claims.paraphrase: IEXT maps each element of IP to a subset of IR × IR; this set of pairs is the property extension.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 3

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every p in IP, IEXT(p) is a set of pairs of elements of IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Subtype membership proofs express the domain and codomain restrictions.

claims.paraphrase: IS maps every IRI into IR ∪ IP.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 4
claims.formalization_note: There is no injectivity or unique-names requirement; different IRIs may denote the same object.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every IRI i, IS(i) belongs to IR union IP.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The source IRI domain is an abstract parameter.

claims.paraphrase: IL is a partial function from literals into IR; a literal may have no denotation.
claims.source_locator: Definition of a simple interpretation, numbered component 5

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: IL is a partial function from literals to IR.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Option encodes undefinedness. It does not identify literals with their denoted values.

claims.paraphrase: A literal evaluates using IL and an IRI using IS.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, first and second rows

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For names, [I+A] agrees with IS on IRIs and IL on literals.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The function is Option-valued because IL is partial.

claims.paraphrase: A ground triple is true precisely when its predicate denotes a member of IP and its subject/object denotations form a pair in that property extension; otherwise it is false.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, third row

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A triple s p o is true under [I+A] exactly when p denotes a property and s and o denote resources whose pair belongs to IEXT of that property.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Undefined denotation makes the existential truth condition false.

claims.paraphrase: A ground graph is true exactly when every member triple is true; one false member makes it false.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for ground graphs, fourth row

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A ground graph G is true exactly when every triple of G is true under I; no blank-node assignment is needed.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: GraphTrue also evaluates non-ground graphs under a specified A. ground_satisfaction proves agreement for ground graphs.

claims.paraphrase: A triple containing a literal with undefined IL is false, and a graph containing that triple is false.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: If IL(l) is undefined, any triple containing l in any position is false, and any graph containing that triple is false.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Covers generalized positions as well as ordinary object literals.

claims.paraphrase: The empty graph is true under every simple interpretation and remains true under conforming semantic extensions wherever their syntax admits it.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Every simple interpretation satisfies the empty graph.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Extension preservation follows when extensions retain the same Satisfies relation and admit empty syntax.

claims.paraphrase: IP and IR may overlap. In a true triple subject/object denotations lie in IR; an IRI used as both predicate and subject/object in a true graph denotes an element of IP ∩ IR.
claims.formalization_note: The dual-role conclusion requires satisfaction of the relevant graph/triples; a false occurrence alone supplies no membership constraint.

claims.paraphrase: An extension may constrain particular IRI denotations, including fixing denotations of recognized datatype IRIs.
For an assignment A from blank nodes to IR, I+A agrees with I on names and with A on its blank-node domain; triple and graph evaluation then uses the ground rules.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A maps exactly the blank nodes occurring in G to IR. [I+A] agrees with A on those blank nodes and with I on names.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A partial ambient-domain function plus exact-domain condition represents the source's function on a subset. Restriction proves that unused extra assignments do not affect satisfaction.

claims.paraphrase: A graph is true under I exactly when there exists one assignment of all its blank nodes to IR that makes the entire graph true.
claims.formalization_note: The existential assignment has whole-graph scope and must be consistent across every occurrence of each blank node; per-triple independent assignments would weaken the condition.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: I satisfies G exactly when one assignment A of G's blank nodes makes every triple in G true.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The existential assignment quantifier is outside the universal triple quantifier.

claims.paraphrase: Blank-node assignments are witnesses to graph truth rather than components of I; blank nodes have no globally fixed denotation under a simple interpretation.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: A blank-node assignment is a witness to graph truth and is not a component of the simple interpretation I.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A structural modelling choice, not a separate theorem about all possible implementations.

claims.paraphrase: Evaluating a list through its set of triples gives the same satisfaction result after permuting or repeating identical triples, while preserving blank-node identity.
claims.formalization_note: This proves a possible set abstraction, not that list length, duplicate-returning scans, or repository APIs refine graph cardinality or unique enumeration.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Lists that denote equal sets of triples have the same graph identity and therefore the same Satisfies proposition.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Set identity is proved; a separately named general list-permutation satisfaction theorem is not yet provided.

claims.paraphrase: Separately satisfying graphs that share a blank node need not satisfy their union; union requires a common witness across those occurrences and changes existential scope.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: There exist an interpretation I and graphs G and H sharing a blank node such that I satisfies G and H separately and their merge, but I does not satisfy their union.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: An abstract two-resource illustration of the informative discussion, not a transcription of the Alice/Bob drawing.

claims.paraphrase: I satisfies E when E evaluates to true; E is satisfiable if some simple interpretation satisfies it and unsatisfiable if none does.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: I satisfies G exactly when G is true under I.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Separate named predicates for satisfiable and unsatisfiable are not yet introduced.

claims.paraphrase: G simply entails E when every simple interpretation satisfying G also satisfies E.
claims.formalization_note: The universal interpretation is shared by premise and conclusion, but their existential blank-node witness assignments need not be the same; joint graph meaning requires union when sharing matters.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: G simply entails E exactly when every simple interpretation satisfying G also satisfies E.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Universe-polymorphic family: all carrier types U in a fixed arbitrary Lean universe u. No claim to quantify over all universes inside one Lean proposition.

claims.paraphrase: Graphs are logically equivalent exactly when each entails the other.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: G and E are logically equivalent exactly when G simply entails E and E simply entails G.

claims.paraphrase: The document does not independently define entailment from a set of graphs; first form a union or merge, choosing whether shared blank-node identities must be retained.
A graph-producing process is simply valid if every output is simply entailed by its corresponding input, and invalid otherwise.

Semantic validity does not require an application to execute an inference, and invalidity does not prohibit a transformation; the specification characterizes truth preservation rather than mandating graph operations.
Entailment preserves truth, not application-specific suitability; properties such as being a usable test manifest need not survive valid entailment.
Every RDF graph has a satisfying simple interpretation; this assertion does not extend automatically to datatype-aware regimes.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: For every graph G, including infinite graphs, there exists a simple interpretation satisfying G.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: A one-element resource/property universe is a witness, not a restriction on the model class.

claims.paraphrase: G simply entails E exactly when an instance of E is a subgraph of G.

Simple entailment is decidable for finite input graphs by searching for a substitution whose image is a subset of the premise; the general problem is computationally hard, while a ground conclusion reduces to subset checking.
claims.formalization_note: The text permits infinite graphs elsewhere; an algorithmic decidability claim requires finite effective input. Appendix A states NP-completeness explicitly.

claims.paraphrase: Every graph simply entails the empty graph, and the empty graph simply entails only itself.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Every graph simply entails the empty graph; if the empty graph simply entails E then E is empty.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: The proof works without finite graphs.

claims.paraphrase: Every graph simply entails each of its subgraphs.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: Every graph simply entails every subgraph of that graph.

claims.paraphrase: Every instance of a graph simply entails that graph.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: If f replaces blank nodes only by blank nodes, the resulting graph G.mapBlank f simply entails G.
cleanroom_mapping.limitations: Only the blank-to-blank case. General substitution by names and interpolation are open.

claims.paraphrase: A lean graph does not simply entail a proper instance of itself.
If S is a subgraph of S-prime and S simply entails E, then S-prime simply entails E.

cleanroom_mapping.symbol_linked_english: If G is a subgraph of H and G simply entails E, then H simply entails E.

claims.paraphrase: If S simply entails a finite E, some finite subset of S already entails E; S itself may be infinite.
claims.formalization_note: Do not replace RDF graph sethood by finiteness without recording the restriction.

claims.paraphrase: A graph cannot simply entail a graph containing an IRI absent from the premise.
Skolemization replaces blank nodes consistently with fresh IRIs coined for this purpose, with distinct blank nodes receiving distinct fresh IRIs.
claims.formalization_note: Freshness is relative to other graphs at creation; the injectivity requirement is explicit in the Appendix C proof.

claims.paraphrase: A skolemized graph simply entails its original graph.
A graph with at least one blank node does not simply entail its skolemization, because the latter introduces a fresh IRI.
claims.formalization_note: The printed statement lacks this nontrivial-skolemization premise; for a ground graph the transformation is identity.

claims.paraphrase: If sk(G) simply entails H, there is H-prime with G entailing H-prime and H = sk(H-prime), using the corresponding inverse replacement of skolem IRIs.
For H containing none of the freshly introduced skolem IRIs, sk(G) simply entails H exactly when G simply entails H.
D is the set of datatype IRIs recognized by an interpretation; recognizing an IRI presupposes determining the unique datatype it identifies.
A recognized datatype IRI identifies the same externally specified datatype at every occurrence; the mechanism establishing that identification is outside this semantics.
The datatype map associated with D is the interpretation restricted to D; descriptions parameterized by a datatype map can use this fixed map.
claims.formalization_note: This definition occurs inside a change note and is therefore informative under section 2.

claims.paraphrase: Literal structure and datatype definitions come from Concepts: ordinary datatype literals pair a lexical string with a datatype IRI; language-tagged strings additionally use a language tag and rdf:langString.
A datatype supplies a lexical space and a partial lexical-to-value mapping; L2V selects that mapping and its range is the value space.
A literal is ill-typed relative to D when its datatype IRI is recognized but its lexical form has no value under the corresponding mapping.
RDF processors need not recognize datatype IRIs beyond rdf:langString and xsd:string; recognizing additional IRIs is permitted.
claims.formalization_note: The minimum is imposed on RDF interpretations in section 8, not on arbitrary simple D-interpretations, where D can be empty.

claims.paraphrase: If a datatype IRI listed in Concepts section 5 is recognized, its specified meaning must be used; recognition of rdf:PlainLiteral requires its separately specified meaning.
When another datatype IRI is recognized, its identification must be unambiguous and remain fixed throughout RDF transformations and manipulations.
rdf:langString identifies a datatype whose values are string/language-tag pairs, with specially defined literal interpretation instead of an L2V mapping.
A literal with an unrecognized datatype IRI should not be rejected solely for that reason and should be treated as denoting some resource like an unknown name; warnings are permitted.
claims.formalization_note: Unknown datatype and recognized datatype with invalid lexical form are different cases. Preserve the SHOULD and MAY force of these statements.

claims.paraphrase: A D-interpretation is a simple interpretation satisfying the additional datatype conditions for its recognized set D.
If rdf:langString belongs to D, each language-tagged literal denotes its lexical string paired with its language tag converted to lowercase by US-ASCII rules.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, first row

claims.paraphrase: For each other IRI in D, its interpretation is the datatype it identifies.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, second row, datatype-denotation conjunct

claims.paraphrase: For a literal typed with a recognized IRI other than rdf:langString, IL is the corresponding lexical-to-value result, including being undefined when that mapping is undefined.
claims.source_locator: Semantic conditions for datatyped literals, second row, literal-value conjunct

claims.paraphrase: Every graph containing an ill-typed literal is false in every D-interpretation; unrecognized datatype IRIs do not create this source of D-unsatisfiability.
Syntactically legal rdf:langString literals always denote when recognized. For xsd:string, the source limits ill-typed forms to strings containing code points outside the XML Char production.
claims.formalization_note: The xsd:string character-domain constraint needs explicit modeling; do not infer that every host-language string is a valid xsd:string value.

claims.paraphrase: D-satisfiability means having at least one satisfying D-interpretation; S D-entails G when every D-interpretation satisfying S also satisfies G.
A graph can lack any satisfying D-interpretation; processors may report this as an error but are not required to do so.
A D-unsatisfiable graph D-entails every graph by the universal-model definition.
claims.formalization_note: This is a vacuous implication over no satisfying models, not an inconsistent interpretation admitted into the model class.

claims.paraphrase: The ex-falso consequence is not an instruction or authorization to produce arbitrary application conclusions from inconsistent data.
With D empty, D-entailment is exactly simple entailment.
The final paragraph states that E-entailment implies D-entailment for D contained in E, and that D-entailment implies simple entailment, while saying more recognized datatypes strengthen entailment.
claims.formalization_note: Recorded as a source claim awaiting review; do not translate it into a trusted theorem without resolving the direction.

claims.paraphrase: With compatible fixed datatype meanings and D contained in E, every E-interpretation is a D-interpretation; therefore D-entailment implies E-entailment, and simple entailment implies D-entailment.
Literals recognized to have the same value can be substituted in corresponding triples to obtain datatype entailments, including across different recognized datatypes with overlapping value spaces.
A fixed generic syntactic pattern set does not capture all datatype entailments; the actual lexical-to-value mappings can supply additional consequences.
Ill-typed literals are the only source of unsatisfiability for simple D-entailment; adding RDF/RDFS vocabulary conditions can introduce other sources.
An RDF interpretation recognizing D is a D-interpretation in which D includes rdf:langString and xsd:string and the RDF conditions and axiomatic triples hold.
x belongs to IP exactly when the pair of x and the denotation of rdf:Property belongs to the extension of rdf:type.
claims.source_locator: RDF semantic condition with HTML identifier rdfsemcond1

claims.paraphrase: For each datatype IRI a in D, rdf:type relates x to I(a) exactly when x belongs to that datatype value space.
claims.source_locator: RDF semantic condition with HTML identifier rdfsemcond3; the source has no rdfsemcond2 row

claims.paraphrase: Each listed RDF vocabulary IRI must satisfy its rdf:type rdf:Property axiomatic triple.
The triple rdf:nil rdf:type rdf:List is true in every RDF interpretation.
For every positive integer n, rdf:_n rdf:type rdf:Property is an RDF axiom.
claims.formalization_note: This is an infinite indexed family; a finite implementation vocabulary needs a justified restriction.

claims.paraphrase: No other special normative meanings are imposed on the remaining RDF vocabulary; recognizing rdf:XMLLiteral and rdf:HTML is optional.

S RDF-entails E recognizing D when every satisfying RDF interpretation of S recognizing D satisfies E; an RDF-unsatisfiable graph has no such model. Unqualified RDF entailment uses D = {rdf:langString, xsd:string}.
The empty graph RDF-entails every RDF axiom, so the simple-entailment interpolation characterization does not extend unchanged to RDF entailment.
From a triple s p literal typed with d in D, infer a graph containing s p b and b rdf:type d for one existential blank node b.
claims.formalization_note: Both conclusion triples use the same witness; the pattern remains semantically valid for an ill-typed premise through unsatisfiability.

claims.paraphrase: From s p o, RDF-entail p rdf:type rdf:Property.
Datatype value spaces can force entailments beyond rdfD1/rdfD2, and incompatible memberships in disjoint recognized datatype value spaces can make a graph RDF-unsatisfiable.
claims.formalization_note: The boolean example uses exhaustiveness of the two boolean values; it cannot be obtained from lexical-value equality alone.

claims.paraphrase: Classes are resources typed rdfs:Class; IC collects them, and ICEXT maps classes to subsets of IR. A class may have an empty extension, and distinct classes can share an extension.
An RDFS interpretation recognizing D is an RDF interpretation recognizing the same D that satisfies the RDFS semantic conditions and axiomatic triples.
ICEXT(y) is the set of x such that rdf:type relates x to y.
IC is ICEXT of the denotation of rdfs:Class.
LV is ICEXT of the denotation of rdfs:Literal.
The extension of rdfs:Resource is exactly IR.
The extension of rdf:langString is exactly the set of denotations of language-tagged literals.
For every other datatype IRI a in D, ICEXT(I(a)) is its value space.
Every recognized datatype denotation belongs to the extension of rdfs:Datatype.
If rdfs:domain relates property x to class y and x relates u to v, then u belongs to ICEXT(y).
If rdfs:range relates property x to class y and x relates u to v, then v belongs to ICEXT(y).
The extension of rdfs:subPropertyOf is transitive on IP.
Every property in IP is related to itself by rdfs:subPropertyOf.
Both endpoints of any rdfs:subPropertyOf pair belong to IP.
If rdfs:subPropertyOf relates x to y, IEXT(x) is a subset of IEXT(y).
claims.formalization_note: The converse is not required; extension inclusion alone does not force a subproperty assertion.

claims.paraphrase: Every class in IC is related to rdfs:Resource by rdfs:subClassOf.
The extension of rdfs:subClassOf is transitive on IC.
Every class in IC is related to itself by rdfs:subClassOf.
Both endpoints of any rdfs:subClassOf pair belong to IC.
claims.source_locator: rdfssemcond7, endpoint-typing conjunct; source order places condition 8 before condition 7

claims.paraphrase: If rdfs:subClassOf relates x to y, ICEXT(x) is a subset of ICEXT(y).
claims.formalization_note: The converse is not required; equal or included class extensions do not by themselves force subclass assertions.

claims.paraphrase: Every member of the rdfs:ContainerMembershipProperty class is a subproperty of rdfs:member.
Every member of the rdfs:Datatype class is a subclass of rdfs:Literal.
Every property/class pair in this family is an axiomatic rdfs:domain triple.
Every property/class pair in this family is an axiomatic rdfs:range triple.
The listed vocabulary hierarchy triples are true in every RDFS interpretation.
For every positive integer n, rdf:_n has type rdfs:ContainerMembershipProperty, domain rdfs:Resource, and range rdfs:Resource.
claims.formalization_note: One uniformly indexed family containing the three corresponding axiom schemas; no finite maximum n is imposed.

claims.paraphrase: IP equals ICEXT(I(rdf:Property)); recognized datatypes act as classes with their value-space extensions, and recognized literals either lack denotation or denote members of those classes.
The source lists these additional rdfs:Class typings as valid in all RDFS interpretations; it explicitly does not claim the list is complete.
The source lists these additional rdf:Property typings as valid in all RDFS interpretations.

Resources, classes and properties are not disjoint categories; class self-membership and property self-application are allowed, while properties of a class do not automatically transfer to its members or conversely.

The meanings of rdfs:comment, rdfs:seeAlso, rdfs:isDefinedBy and rdfs:label are constrained only through their specified domain/range/subproperty uses. The axiom/condition set intentionally contains redundancy.
claims.formalization_note: The inventory does not require redundant source assertions to become independent implementation mechanisms.

claims.paraphrase: RDFS domain or range consequences can force an individual into disjoint recognized datatype classes and thereby make a graph unsatisfiable.
A dataset has one default graph and zero or more named graphs under the Concepts definition; component graphs may share blank nodes.
A graph name used as an RDF term need not denote its associated graph, and engines should not presume that relationship without an external reason.
A dataset may be used to express RDF content; when it is, it should carry at least the semantic content of its default graph.
claims.formalization_note: MAY and SHOULD do not define a complete, uniquely mandated dataset entailment relation.

claims.paraphrase: Replacing the default graph by a logically equivalent graph need not preserve dataset structure or cross-graph blank-node sharing.
claims.formalization_note: The paragraph starts with an ordinary prose caution, not a styled note; structural isomorphism and logical equivalence remain distinct.

claims.paraphrase: Semantic extensions may impose further dataset meaning and restrictions; comparing corresponding named graphs is an example rather than the required core semantics.
The ordinary rule-based check augments the premise with relevant axioms, saturates it with inference patterns, then tests whether some instance of the conclusion is included.
claims.formalization_note: The appendix is informative; this procedure is not a mandatory implementation architecture.

procedure_steps.operation: Add all RDF or RDF+RDFS axiomatic triples that do not contain container membership IRIs.
Add axioms containing each container membership IRI that occurs in the conclusion.
Apply the appropriate RDF/RDFS inference patterns until no new triples are produced.
Check whether the enlarged graph contains an instance of the conclusion.

claims.paraphrase: A positive result from the ordinary-syntax procedure establishes entailment, but some valid RDF/RDFS entailments are missed.
claims.formalization_note: The examples expose shared datatype witnesses and intermediate blank-node predicates; implementing every displayed rule on legal RDF triples alone does not establish completeness.

claims.paraphrase: For a premise triple containing a literal typed by d in D, infer the generalized triple literal rdf:type d.

The generalized RDF/RDFS closure of S towards E adds the prescribed finite-vocabulary axioms and saturates generalized triples with GrdfD1, rdfD2 and, for RDFS, rdfs1–rdfs13 at the base recognized datatype set.

procedure_steps.operation: Add RDF or RDF+RDFS axioms not containing a container membership IRI.
For every container membership IRI in E, add the axioms containing it.
If step 2 added no triples, add the axioms containing rdf:_1.
Saturate under GrdfD1 and rdfD2, plus rdfs1–rdfs13 for RDFS, with D = {rdf:langString, xsd:string}.

claims.paraphrase: If S is RDF-consistent, respectively RDFS-consistent, then S entails E in that regime exactly when the corresponding generalized closure towards E simply entails E.
claims.formalization_note: Retain the consistency premise, regime-specific closure and base datatype set. This theorem does not automatically cover arbitrary additional datatypes or inconsistent inputs.

claims.paraphrase: For finite effective input, the generalized closure is finite and its generation is decidable with polynomial complexity.
claims.formalization_note: The source states finite closures without restating a finite-input premise; an infinite S cannot have a finite closure containing it. This is a scope question, not a confirmed erratum.

claims.paraphrase: Simple entailment is NP-complete in general for finite inputs, while a conclusion without blank nodes admits a low-order polynomial check.
claims.formalization_note: Keep the complexity of closure generation separate from the subsequent existential substitution search.

claims.paraphrase: A practical subset of the rules can miss consequences; replacing GrdfD1 with legal-syntax rdfD1 also loses completeness. Larger recognized datatype sets require datatype-specific reasoning.
A pre-interpretation uses a restricted vocabulary V and maps only names in that vocabulary, enabling smaller semantic structures for the graphs being compared.
The sketch restricts to the names in G union E and gives a resource bound N+B+1, where N counts names and B counts blank nodes, with extensions preserving relevant triple truth values.
claims.formalization_note: This is an informative sketch without proof, for finite compared vocabularies; the exact treatment of unmentioned terms remains a formalization obligation.

claims.paraphrase: For datatype entailment, the sketch weakens value requirements to literals occurring in the compared graphs and gives the bound (N+B)×(D+1), with D here counting recognized datatypes.
claims.formalization_note: The cardinality D in the bound is not a multiplication of the datatype-IRI set; finite datatype-set assumptions must be explicit.

claims.paraphrase: For RDF/RDFS, the sketch restricts container vocabulary and relevant literal values, and claims suitable finite pre-interpretations extend to full interpretations without changing truth or entailment for the compared graphs.

claims.paraphrase: Much reification, container and collection intent is deliberately omitted from the formal semantic conditions; the appendix discusses intended use rather than adding mandatory entailments.
Reification uses rdf:Statement, rdf:subject, rdf:predicate and rdf:object to describe an RDF triple token or concrete realization.
Reification relates a triple token to the resources its components denote, rather than quoting the component IRIs as syntactic objects.
Reifying a triple does not entail asserting it, and asserting a triple does not entail the existence of its reification.
Multiple reifications can describe matching components without denoting the same token; properties asserted of one such entity need not transfer to another.
Container vocabulary describes entities with a type and partial membership information; indexed membership properties distinguish positions, while rdfs:member is generic membership.

The informal intended uses are an unordered duplicate-permitting bag, an ordered sequence, and alternatives that may have a preference order; indexed properties are intended as single-valued positions.
claims.formalization_note: These intended properties are not additional formal RDF entailment conditions. Permitting duplicate bag members is not permitting repeated identical triples in an RDF graph.

claims.paraphrase: The bag interpretation does not justify permuting indexed membership assertions as an RDF entailment.
A property of a container does not automatically hold of its members, nor does a member property automatically hold of the container.
Formal semantics does not require container classes to be disjoint or indexed positions to be gap-free; RDF supplies no fixed upper membership bound or general finiteness requirement.
claims.formalization_note: These are absences of special constraints, not requirements that every application accept every intended container shape.

claims.paraphrase: Collection vocabulary describes head/tail structures using rdf:first and rdf:rest with rdf:nil as a terminator; the usual application convention follows the rest chain to enumerate items.
Beyond existing RDF/RDFS conditions, collection vocabulary has no special well-formedness constraints; branching tails, multiple heads and missing rest information are possible RDF descriptions.
A described collection does not force the existence of every permutation or other derived collection; naming one sequence does not entail a newly ordered sequence.
An extension may impose collection syntax and interpretation conditions selecting well-formed chains whose values form an ordered sequence, including sequences containing other sequences.
Under RDFS, every rdf:first subject and every rdf:rest subject or object has type rdf:List by the existing domain/range constraints.
